title: Fabric Implementation Delivery Chain — Environments to Operational Readiness
purpose: Shows the reference delivery phases for a Fabric implementation, from workspace environments through deployment pipelines, testing, security controls, and finally operational readiness — grounded in documented deployment-pipeline, mirroring, private-link, and item-recovery behavior.
accessibleSummary: A five-phase horizontal delivery chain. Dev, Test, and Production workspace environments feed Fabric deployment pipelines, which promote items and inject environment-specific configuration through Variable Libraries behind a pull-request gate. Promoted items then pass through a testing phase that validates data quality and, for mirrored items, must manually trigger replication because promotion alone leaves the target item empty. A security phase applies workspace and tenant-level access controls, with a warning that Deployment Pipelines and Fabric SQL Database stop working entirely if public access is blocked at the workspace or private links are enabled tenant-wide. The chain ends at operational readiness, where Item Recovery's up-to-90-day retention window and monitoring evidence gate whether the release is accepted. A feedback edge routes failed acceptance back to the environments phase.
longDescription: This is a reference implementation path for standing up a governed Fabric delivery process, not a single Microsoft-documented end-to-end diagram — it composes five phases that are each independently grounded: workspace environments, Deployment Pipelines promotion (with Variable Libraries and PR gates), a testing phase that must account for mirroring's manual-replication-trigger behavior, a security phase built on the documented workspace- and tenant-level public-access/private-link restrictions that specifically disable Deployment Pipelines and Fabric SQL Database, and an operational-readiness phase built on Item Recovery's GA retention window. The composition and sequencing of these phases into one delivery chain is this diagram's own architectural interpretation (pattern/inference), while each phase's internal behavior is sourced.

nodes.label: Workspace environments (Dev / Test / Production)
nodes.summary: Three workspaces — Dev, Test, and Production — form the promotion chain that deployment pipelines move items across.
nodes.detail: A Fabric deployment pipeline assigns Dev, Test, and Production workspace stages and promotes items between them in order. Each stage is a distinct workspace with its own capacity assignment, permissions, and connections, so items behave the same structurally at every stage while their configuration differs per environment.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without separate workspace stages, there is no boundary between work-in-progress items and the ones consumers depend on, and no place for deployment pipelines to promote between.

inputs: Workspace naming and capacity assignment plan
processing: Provision Dev, Test, and Production workspaces
Assign each to an appropriately sized capacity
Restrict write access to Production to the deployment pipeline identity
outputs: Three staged workspaces ready for pipeline assignment
drill.example: A sales analytics team provisions fabric-sales-dev, fabric-sales-test, and fabric-sales-prod, with only the deployment pipeline service principal holding write access to fabric-sales-prod.
controls: Naming convention for pipeline stage matching
failureModes: Developers push directly to the Production workspace, bypassing the pipeline
Test workspace under-provisioned relative to Production, hiding capacity issues until release

nodes.label: Deployment Pipelines — promote + Variable Libraries
nodes.summary: Deployment Pipelines promotes items across Dev, Test, and Production while Variable Libraries swap in environment-specific connection strings, gated by a pull request.
nodes.detail: The documented delivery pattern uses Fabric Deployment Pipelines to promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, with Variable Libraries injecting environment-specific connection strings so the same item definition targets a different source or destination per stage, and a pull-request gate required before promotion to Production.
nodes.whyItMatters: Promotion without environment-scoped variables forces manual post-deploy edits in Production, and promotion without a PR gate removes the last human checkpoint before a change reaches consumers.

evidence.note: Recommends a deployment pattern using Deployment Pipelines to promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, with Variable Libraries injecting environment-specific connection strings, and pull-request gates required before promotion to production.
Deployment pipelines are used for promoting an item from development to production workspaces, alongside Git integration for version control.

inputs: Items validated in the Dev workspace
Variable Library values per target stage
processing: Compare source and target stage content
Substitute stage-specific variable values on promotion
Block the Production promotion until the PR gate is satisfied
outputs: Promoted items in the next stage workspace
An audit record of what was promoted and by whom
drill.example: A warehouse item promoted from Test to Production automatically repoints its connection string at the production source system via a Variable Library entry, without editing the item's definition by hand.
controls: Variable Library value sets per stage
Required PR reviewers before Production promotion
failureModes: Missing a stage-specific variable value, so promotion silently carries over a Dev connection string
Promoting without a merged PR because the gate is only a convention, not an enforced branch policy

nodes.label: Testing — quality gates + mirroring replication trigger
nodes.summary: Promoted items are validated for quality before serving, and any mirrored database item needs its replication triggered manually since promotion alone leaves it empty.
nodes.detail: After Deployment Pipelines promotes a mirrored database item into a target workspace, replication does not start automatically — the target receives a configured but empty item, and an operator must manually trigger replication, which performs a full initial load from the current source state. Any testing phase that includes mirrored items must account for this manual step or tests will run against empty data.
nodes.whyItMatters: A pipeline that reports a successful deployment can still hand testing an empty mirrored table; without knowing this behavior, a team wastes time debugging what looks like a data bug but is actually a missed manual trigger.

evidence.note: After a deployment pipeline deploys a mirrored database item to a target workspace, replication does not start automatically; the target receives a configured but empty item and an operator must manually trigger replication, which performs a complete initial load.

inputs: Freshly promoted items in the Test (or Production) workspace
Data quality assertions and row-count/schema checks
processing: Manually trigger replication on any promoted mirrored item before testing its data
Run schema and row-level quality checks against promoted items
Compare test-run output against expected baselines
outputs: Pass/fail quality evidence per promoted item
A replicating (not empty) mirrored database ready for downstream reads
drill.example: A mirrored operational database promoted to Test shows zero rows until an operator manually starts replication, after which quality checks can run against the full initial load.
controls: Manual or scripted replication-trigger step in the release runbook
failureModes: Quality checks run and 'pass' against an empty mirrored table because zero rows trivially satisfies a null-check
No runbook step for triggering replication, so testing is silently skipped for mirrored items

nodes.label: Security — workspace & tenant access controls
nodes.summary: Workspace-level Block Public Access and tenant-level private links are real architectural trade-offs: both disable Deployment Pipelines and Fabric SQL Database outright, not just restrict them.
nodes.detail: At the workspace level, Fabric SQL Database, Deployment Pipelines, shortcut transforms, and the Power Platform Dataflow Connector are all unsupported when public access is blocked on the workspace — a design-level constraint, not a configuration gap. Tenant-level private links are a viable choice only for pure cloud-to-cloud workloads on F SKUs with no dependency on on-premises sources, Deployment Pipelines, or Fabric SQL Database, and where the resulting Power BI feature limitations are operationally acceptable.
nodes.whyItMatters: Enabling a network-security control that seems purely additive can silently remove the CI/CD mechanism this whole delivery chain depends on, so security decisions have to be made with the deployment pipeline's requirements in view, not after the fact.

evidence.note: At the workspace level, Fabric SQL Database, Deployment Pipelines, shortcut transforms, and the Power Platform Dataflow Connector are all unsupported when public access is blocked on the workspace — a design-level constraint, unlikely to be resolved by minor product updates.

Private links are a viable architectural choice only for pure cloud-to-cloud workloads on F SKUs with no dependency on on-premises sources, Deployment Pipelines, or Fabric SQL Database, and where Power BI feature limitations are acceptable.

inputs: List of items the delivery chain depends on (Deployment Pipelines, Fabric SQL Database, shortcuts)
processing: Check whether the workspace or tenant depends on Deployment Pipelines or Fabric SQL Database before restricting public access
Confirm on-premises gateway dependency is absent before enabling tenant-level private links
Document the accepted Power BI feature trade-offs if private links are enabled
outputs: A network-security posture that keeps the delivery chain functional, or an explicit documented decision to lose Deployment Pipelines
drill.example: A team that needs Deployment Pipelines to promote a Fabric SQL Database item cannot also block public access on that workspace — the two requirements are mutually exclusive by design.
controls: Documented exception process for teams that must choose isolation over Deployment Pipelines
failureModes: Security team enables Block Public Access tenant-wide without checking Deployment Pipelines usage, breaking every team's release process at once
On-premises gateways silently stop registering after tenant-level private links are enabled, since no supported configuration lets both coexist

nodes.label: Operational readiness — Item Recovery + monitoring gate
nodes.summary: Release is accepted only once monitoring evidence exists and the Item Recovery retention window is confirmed as the safety net for the newly promoted items.
nodes.detail: Item Recovery reached General Availability and lets tenant admins configure a retention window of up to 90 days, adjustable at any time; deleted items can be restored via the Workspace Recycle bin or the REST API within that window, after which a soft-deleted item is permanently and unrecoverably deleted. Operational readiness for a release means confirming this recovery window is set appropriately and that monitoring/alerting evidence exists for the newly promoted items before calling the release complete.
nodes.whyItMatters: A release that has passed quality gates but has no confirmed recovery window or monitoring in place is one accidental deletion or unnoticed failure away from being unrecoverable or invisible.

evidence.note: Tenant admins can configure a retention window of up to 90 days for Item Recovery and can adjust that window at any time; deleted items can be restored via the Workspace Recycle bin or REST API within that window.

inputs: Promoted, tested, and security-reviewed Production items
Monitoring and alerting coverage for the release
processing: Confirm the tenant's Item Recovery retention window meets the release's recovery objective
Verify monitoring and alerting are wired to the newly promoted items
Sign off the release as operationally accepted
outputs: An accepted release with a confirmed recovery window and monitoring coverage
Operational runbook entry for the release
drill.example: A release owner confirms the tenant's 30-day Item Recovery window covers the team's recovery point objective before accepting a Production promotion, and verifies a failed-run alert is wired to the on-call channel.
controls: Tenant Item Recovery retention window setting
failureModes: A team assumes indefinite recovery and only discovers the retention window after the recovery point has already expired
Release accepted with no monitoring wired up, so the first sign of failure is a user complaint

edges.label: quality-passed items proceed to access review
Block Public Access / tenant private links disable Deployment Pipelines
failed acceptance sends the release back to Dev

walkthrough.title: 1. Stage the environments
walkthrough.explanation: Provision Dev, Test, and Production workspaces that a deployment pipeline can promote items across.

walkthrough.title: 2. Promote through CI/CD
walkthrough.explanation: Deployment Pipelines promotes items, Variable Libraries swap environment-specific configuration, and a pull-request gate protects Production.

walkthrough.title: 3. Test the promoted release
walkthrough.explanation: Validate data quality — and manually trigger replication on any promoted mirrored item, since promotion alone leaves it empty.

walkthrough.title: 4. Apply security controls
walkthrough.explanation: Workspace Block Public Access and tenant-level private links are real trade-offs that can disable Deployment Pipelines and Fabric SQL Database outright.

walkthrough.title: 5. Confirm operational readiness
walkthrough.explanation: Accept the release only once the Item Recovery retention window and monitoring evidence are confirmed.
